Albert Arnold Gore Jr. was born on March 31, 1948, in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-14) as the second of two children born to [Albert Gore Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Gore_Sr. "Albert Gore Sr."), a U.S. Representative who later served for 18 years as a U.S. Senator from Tennessee, and [Pauline LaFon Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_LaFon_Gore "Pauline LaFon Gore"), one of the first women to graduate from the [Vanderbilt University Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Law_School "Vanderbilt University Law School").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15) Gore is a descendant of [Scots Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch-Irish_Americans "Scotch-Irish Americans") immigrants who first settled in [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") during the mid-17th-century and moved to Tennessee after the [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-16) His older sister Nancy LaFon Gore died of lung cancer in 1984.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-pbschron-17)

During the school year he lived with his family in The Fairfax Hotel in the [Embassy Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_Row "Embassy Row") section in Washington D.C.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-twoworlds-18) During the summer months, he worked on the family farm in [Carthage, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage,_Tennessee "Carthage, Tennessee"), where the Gores grew tobacco and hay[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-farm-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-dc-20) and raised cattle.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-21)

Gore attended [St. Albans School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Albans_School_(Washington,_D.C.) "St. Albans School (Washington, D.C.)"), an independent college preparatory day and boarding school for boys in Washington, D.C., from 1956 to 1965, a prestigious feeder school for the [Ivy League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy_League "Ivy League").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) He was the captain of the football team, [threw discus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discus_throw "Discus throw") for the track and field team and participated in basketball, art, and government.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-twoworlds-18)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-albans-24) He graduated 25th in a class of 51, applied to one college, [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), and was accepted.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23)

### Harvard

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Albert_Gore_Sr._speaking_at_the_1968_DNC.jpg/250px-Albert_Gore_Sr._speaking_at_the_1968_DNC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Albert_Gore_Sr._speaking_at_the_1968_DNC.jpg)

Albert Gore Sr. delivering a speech to the [1968 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention "1968 Democratic National Convention") which the younger Gore helped him write

Gore enrolled in [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College") in 1965; he initially planned to [major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_major "Academic major") in [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_studies "English studies") and write novels but later decided to major in government.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) On his second day on campus, he began campaigning for the [freshman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshman "Freshman") student government council and was elected its president. He was roommates with future actor [Tommy Lee Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Lee_Jones "Tommy Lee Jones") in [Dunster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunster_House "Dunster House").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-25)

Gore was an avid reader who fell in love with scientific and mathematical theories,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) but he did not do well in science classes and avoided taking math.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22) During his first two years, his grades placed him in the lower one-fifth of his class. During his second year, he reportedly spent much of his time watching television, [shooting pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_sport "Cue sport") and occasionally smoking [marijuana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marijuana "Marijuana").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) In his junior and senior years, he became more involved with his studies, earning As and Bs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22) In his senior year, he took a class with oceanographer and global warming theorist [Roger Revelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Revelle "Roger Revelle"), who sparked Gore's interest in global warming and other environmental issues.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-26) Gore earned an A on his thesis, "The Impact of Television on the Conduct of the Presidency, 1947–1969", and graduated with an [A.B.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelors_of_Arts "Bachelors of Arts")_[cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cum\_laude "Cum laude")_ in June 1969.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gore's_Grades-22)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-27)

Gore was in college during the era of anti-[Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") protests. He was opposed to the war but disagreed with the tactics of the student [protest movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_movement "Protest movement"), and believed it to be juvenile and misguided to use a private university as a venue to vent anger at the war.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) He and his friends did not participate in Harvard demonstrations. John Tyson, a former roommate, recalled, "We distrusted these movements a lot ... We were a pretty traditional bunch of guys, positive for civil rights and women's rights but formal, transformed by the social revolution to some extent but not buying into something we considered detrimental to our country."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-frosh-28)

Gore and his sister, Nancy, accompanied their parents to the [1968 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention "1968 Democratic National Convention") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). With his father being a senator, his family had tickets to sit inside of the convention hall at the [International Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Amphitheatre "International Amphitheatre").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Carolll1968_1968_Violence_in_Chicago_Left_Mark-29) He helped write an anti-war address that his father delivered to the convention.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) While at the convention, Gore witnessed some of [the protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention_protests "1968 Democratic National Convention protests") in the streets,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Carolll1968_1968_Violence_in_Chicago_Left_Mark-29) but remained with his parents inside of their hotel room when violence erupted at the protests.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23)

## Military service and early career (1969–1976)

### Military service

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/AlGoreVietnam.png/250px-AlGoreVietnam.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AlGoreVietnam.png)

Gore with the [20th Engineer Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Engineer_Brigade "20th Engineer Brigade") in [Biên Hòa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi%C3%AAn_H%C3%B2a "Biên Hòa") as a journalist with the paper _The Castle Courier_

When Gore graduated in 1969, he immediately became eligible for the [military draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_the_United_States "Conscription in the United States"). His father, a vocal anti-Vietnam War critic, was facing re-election [in 1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_United_States_Senate_election_in_Tennessee "1970 United States Senate election in Tennessee"). Gore eventually decided that enlisting in the Army would be the best course between serving his country, his personal values and interests. Although nearly all of his Harvard classmates avoided the draft and service in Vietnam,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-serveornot-30) Gore believed if he found a way around military service, he would be handing an issue to his father's Republican opponent.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-mixed-31) According to Gore's Senate biography, "He appeared in uniform in his father's campaign commercials, one of which ended with his father advising: 'Son, always love your country'."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) Despite this, Gore Sr. lost the election to an opponent who vastly out-fundraised him. This opponent was later found by the Watergate commission to have accepted illegal money from Nixon's operatives.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-mixed-31)

Gore has said that his other reason for enlisting was that he did not want someone with fewer options than he to go in his place.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-campaign_portrait-33) Actor [Tommy Lee Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Lee_Jones "Tommy Lee Jones"), a former college housemate, recalled Gore saying that "if he found a fancy way of not going, someone else would have to go in his place".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-tells-34) His Harvard advisor, [Richard Neustadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Neustadt "Richard Neustadt"), also stated that Gore decided, "that he would have to go as an enlisted man because, he said, 'In Tennessee, that's what most people have to do.'" In addition, Michael Roche, Gore's editor for _The Castle Courier_, stated that "anybody who knew Al Gore in Vietnam knows he could have sat on his butt and he didn't."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-mixed-31)

After enlisting in August 1969, Gore returned to the anti war Harvard campus in his military uniform to say goodbye to his adviser and was "jeered" at by students.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-pbschron-17)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) He later said he was astonished by the "emotional field of negativity and disapproval and piercing glances that ... certainly felt like real hatred".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-harvardnyt-23) Gore had basic training at [Fort Dix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Dix "Fort Dix") from August to October, and then was assigned to be a journalist at [Fort Rucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Rucker "Fort Rucker"), Alabama.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-mixed-31) In April 1970, he was named Rucker's "Soldier of the Month".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-pbschron-17)

His orders to be sent to Vietnam were "held up" for some time and the Gore family suspected that this was due to a fear by the [Nixon administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_administration "Nixon administration") that if something happened to him, his father would gain sympathy votes.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-mixed-31) He was finally shipped to [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Vietnam "South Vietnam") on January 2, 1971, after his father had lost his seat in the Senate during the [1970 Senate election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_United_States_Senate_elections "1970 United States Senate elections"), becoming one "of only about a dozen of the 1,115 Harvard graduates in the [all-male] Class of '69 who went to Vietnam".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-mixed-31)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-boy-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-father-36) Gore was stationed with the [20th Engineer Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Engineer_Brigade "20th Engineer Brigade") in [Biên Hòa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi%C3%AAn_H%C3%B2a "Biên Hòa") and was a journalist with _The Castle Courier._[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-cc-37) He received an [honorable discharge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_discharge "Military discharge") from the Army in May 1971.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-pbschron-17) Of his time in the Army, Gore later stated, "I didn't do the most, or run the gravest danger. But I was proud to wear my country's uniform."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-tells-34) He also later stated that his experience in Vietnam

> didn't change my conclusions about the war being a terrible mistake, but it struck me that opponents to the war, including myself, really did not take into account the fact that there were an awful lot of [South Vietnamese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Vietnamese "South Vietnamese") who desperately wanted to hang on to what they called freedom. Coming face to face with those sentiments expressed by people who did the laundry and ran the restaurants and worked in the fields was something I was naively unprepared for.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-38)

### Vanderbilt and journalism

Gore was "dispirited" after his return from Vietnam.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) The _[Nashville Scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_Scene "Nashville Scene")_ later noted that "his father's defeat made service in a conflict he deeply opposed even more abhorrent to Gore. His experiences in the war zone don't seem to have been deeply traumatic in themselves; although the engineers were sometimes fired upon, Gore has said he didn't see full-scale combat. Still, he felt that his participation in the war was wrong."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-boy-35) Although his parents wanted him to go to law school, Gore first attended [Vanderbilt University Divinity School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Divinity_School "Vanderbilt University Divinity School") (1971–1972) on a [Rockefeller Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Foundation "Rockefeller Foundation") scholarship for people planning secular careers. He later said he went there in order to explore "spiritual issues",[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-CNN-990616-39) and that "he had hoped to make sense of the social injustices that seemed to challenge his religious beliefs".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Spiritual_Search-40)

In 1971, Gore began to work the night shift for _[The Tennessean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tennessean "The Tennessean")_ as an [investigative reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_reporter "Investigative reporter").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-congressbio-41) His investigations of corruption among members of [Nashville's Metro Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville's_Metro_Council "Nashville's Metro Council") resulted in the arrest and prosecution of two councilmen for separate offenses.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-boy-35) In 1974, he took a leave of absence from _The Tennessean_ to attend [Vanderbilt University Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Law_School "Vanderbilt University Law School"). His decision to become an attorney was a partial result of his time as a journalist, as he realized that, while he could expose corruption, he could not change it.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-CNN-990616-39) Gore did not complete law school, deciding abruptly in 1976 to run for a seat in the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") when he found out that his father's former seat in the House was about to be vacated.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-CNN-990616-39)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-decision-42)

## Congressional career (1977–1993)

See also: [Electoral history of Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_history_of_Al_Gore "Electoral history of Al Gore"), [Al Gore and information technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore_and_information_technology "Al Gore and information technology"), and [Environmental activism of Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_activism_of_Al_Gore "Environmental activism of Al Gore")

Gore began serving in the U.S. Congress at the age of 28 and stayed there for the next 16 years, serving in both the House (1977–1985) and the Senate (1985–1993).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-congressbio-41) Gore spent many weekends in Tennessee, working with his constituents.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Al_Gore_Senate_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Al_Gore_Senate_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Al_Gore_Senate_portrait_(cropped).jpg)

Gore's portrait as Senator 

### House and Senate

At the end of February 1976, U.S. Representative [Joe L. Evins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_L._Evins "Joe L. Evins") unexpectedly announced his retirement from Congress, making [Tennessee's 4th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee's_4th_congressional_district "Tennessee's 4th congressional district") seat, to which he had succeeded Albert Gore Sr. in 1953, [open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent "Incumbent"). Within hours after _The Tennessean_ publisher [John Seigenthaler Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Seigenthaler_Sr. "John Seigenthaler Sr.") called him to tell him the announcement was forthcoming,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-decision-42) Gore decided to quit law school and run for the House of Representatives:

> Gore's abrupt decision to run for the open seat surprised even himself; he later said that "I didn't realize myself I had been pulled back so much to it." The news came as a "bombshell" to his wife. Tipper Gore held a job in _The Tennessean_'s photo lab and was working on a master's degree in psychology, but she joined in her husband's campaign (with assurance that she could get her job at _The Tennessean_ back if he lost). By contrast, Gore asked his father to stay out of his campaign: "I must become my own man," he explained. "I must not be your candidate."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)

Gore won the 1976 Democratic primary for the district with "32 percent of the vote, three percentage points more than his nearest rival", and was opposed by only an independent candidate in the election, recording 94 percent of the overall vote.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-traveler-43) He went on to win the next three elections, in [1978](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "1978 United States House of Representatives elections"), [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "1980 United States House of Representatives elections") and [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "1982 United States House of Representatives elections"), where "he was unopposed twice and won 79 percent of the vote the other time".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-traveler-43)[In 1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_United_States_Senate_election_in_Tennessee "1984 United States Senate election in Tennessee"), Gore successfully ran for a seat in the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Tennessee "List of United States senators from Tennessee"), which had been vacated by Republican [Senate Majority Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_Senate "Party leaders of the United States Senate")[Howard Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Baker "Howard Baker"). He was "unopposed in the Democratic Senatorial primary and won the general election going away", despite the fact that Republican President Ronald Reagan swept Tennessee in his [reelection campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_United_States_presidential_election "1984 United States presidential election") the same year.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-traveler-43) Gore defeated Republican senatorial nominee [Victor Ashe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Ashe "Victor Ashe"), subsequently the [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Knoxville,_Tennessee "List of mayors of Knoxville, Tennessee") of [Knoxville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knoxville,_Tennessee "Knoxville, Tennessee"), and the Republican-turned-[Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_(politics) "Independent (politics)"), [Ed McAteer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_McAteer "Ed McAteer"), founder of the [Christian right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_right "Christian right") Religious Roundtable organization that had worked to elect Reagan as president in 1980.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-44)

During his time in Congress, Gore was considered a moderate, once referring to himself as a "raging moderate",[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-rm-45) opposing federal funding of abortion, voting in favor of a bill which supported a moment of silence in schools, and voting against a ban on interstate sales of guns.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-longest-46) In 1981, Gore was quoted as saying with regard to homosexuality, "I think it is wrong", and "I don't pretend to understand it, but it is not just another normal optional life style." In his 1984 Senate race, Gore said when discussing homosexuality, "I do not believe it is simply an acceptable alternative that society should affirm." He also said that he would not take campaign funds from [gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_rights "Gay rights") groups.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-47) Although he maintained a position against homosexuality and [gay marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_marriage "Gay marriage") in the 1980s, Gore said in 2008 that he thinks "gay men and women ought to have the same rights as heterosexual men and women...to join together in marriage."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-48) His position as a moderate (and on policies related to that label) shifted later in life after he became [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Presidency_of_Al_Gore "Vice Presidency of Al Gore") and [ran for president in 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore_presidential_campaign,_2000 "Al Gore presidential campaign, 2000").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-aim-49)

During his tenure in the House, Gore voted in favor of the [bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passage_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr._Day "Passage of Martin Luther King Jr. Day") establishing [Martin Luther King Jr. Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr._Day "Martin Luther King Jr. Day") as a [federal holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_holidays_in_the_United_States "Federal holidays in the United States").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-50) While Gore initially did not vote on the [Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Restoration_Act_of_1987 "Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987") in January 1988,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-51) he voted to override [President Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s veto the following March.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-52) Gore voted against the nomination of [William Rehnquist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rehnquist#Chief_Justice "William Rehnquist") as [Chief Justice of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States "Chief Justice of the United States"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-53) as well as the nominations of [Robert Bork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination "Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination") and [Clarence Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination") to the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-54)

During his time in the House, Gore sat on the [Energy and Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Energy_and_Commerce "United States House Committee on Energy and Commerce") and the [Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Science_and_Technology "United States House Committee on Science and Technology") committees, chairing the Science Committee's Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations for four years.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-traveler-43) He also sat on the [House Intelligence Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Permanent_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence") and, in 1982, introduced the _Gore Plan_ for [arms control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_control "Arms control"), to "reduce chances of a nuclear first strike by cutting multiple warheads and deploying single-warhead mobile launchers".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) While in the Senate, he sat on the [Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Homeland_Security_and_Governmental_Affairs "United States Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs"), the [Rules and Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Rules_and_Administration "United States Senate Committee on Rules and Administration"), and the [Armed Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Armed_Services "United States Senate Committee on Armed Services") Committees.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) In 1991, Gore was one of ten Democrats who supported the [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)

Gore was considered one of the _[Atari Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari\_Democrat "Atari Democrat")_, given this name due to their "passion for technological issues, from biomedical research and genetic engineering to the environmental impact of the "[greenhouse effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_effect "Greenhouse effect")".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) On March 19, 1979, he had become the first member of Congress to appear on [C-SPAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-SPAN "C-SPAN").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-cspan-55) During this time, Gore co-chaired the Congressional Clearinghouse on the Future with [Newt Gingrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newt_Gingrich "Newt Gingrich").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-56) In addition, he has been described as having been a "genuine nerd, with a geek reputation running back to his days as a futurist _Atari Democrat_ in the House. Before computers were comprehensible, let alone sexy, the poker-faced Gore struggled to explain [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") and [fiber-optic networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber-optic_network "Fiber-optic network") to sleepy colleagues."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-challange-57) Internet pioneers [Vint Cerf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vint_Cerf "Vint Cerf") and [Bob Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Kahn "Bob Kahn") noted that,

> as far back as the 1970s, Congressman Gore promoted the idea of high-speed telecommunications as an engine for both economic growth and the improvement of our educational system. He was the first elected official to grasp the potential of computer communications to have a broader impact than just improving the conduct of science and scholarship ... the Internet, as we know it today, was not deployed until 1983. When the Internet was still in the early stages of its deployment, Congressman Gore provided intellectual leadership by helping create the vision of the potential benefits of high-speed computing and communication.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-cerfkahn-58)

Gore introduced the Supercomputer Network Study Act of 1986.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Gregory-59) He also sponsored hearings on how advanced technologies might be put to use in areas like coordinating the response of government agencies to natural disasters and other crises.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-cerfkahn-58) As a Senator, Gore began to craft the _[High Performance Computing Act of 1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High\_Performance\_Computing\_Act\_of\_1991 "High Performance Computing Act of 1991")_ (commonly referred to as "The Gore Bill") after hearing the 1988 report _Toward a National Research Network_ submitted to Congress by a group chaired by [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA") professor of computer science, [Leonard Kleinrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Kleinrock "Leonard Kleinrock"), one of the central creators of the [ARPANET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET#ARPA_deployed "ARPANET") (the ARPANET, first deployed by Kleinrock and others in 1969, is the predecessor of the Internet).[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-61)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-62) The bill was passed on December 9, 1991, and led to the [National Information Infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Information_Infrastructure "National Information Infrastructure") (NII) which Gore referred to as the "[information superhighway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_superhighway "Information superhighway")".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-63) After joining the House of Representatives, Gore held the "first congressional hearings on the climate change, and co-sponsor[ed] hearings on toxic waste and global warming".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-guadiantimeline-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-nation-65) He continued to speak on the topic throughout the 1980s.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-timegreen-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-nytgreen-67) In 1990, Senator Gore presided over a three-day conference with legislators from over 42 countries which sought to create a _[Global Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global\_Marshall\_Plan "Global Marshall Plan"),_ "under which industrial nations would help less developed countries grow economically while still protecting the environment".[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Shabecoff1990-68)

### Son's 1989 accident and first book

On April 3, 1989, Al, Tipper and their six-year-old son Albert were leaving a baseball game. Albert ran across the street to see his friend and was hit by a car. He was thrown 30 feet (9 m) and then traveled along the pavement for another 20 feet (6 m).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15) Gore later recalled: "I ran to his side and held him and called his name, but he was motionless, limp and still, without breath or pulse.... His eyes were open with the nothingness stare of death, and we prayed, the two of us, there in the gutter, with only my voice."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15) Albert was tended to by two nurses who happened to be present during the accident. The Gores spent the next month in the hospital with Albert. Gore also commented: "Our lives were consumed with the struggle to restore his body and spirit."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15) This event was "a trauma so shattering that [Gore] views it as a moment of personal rebirth", a "key moment in his life" which "changed everything".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-women-15)

In August 1991, Gore announced that his son's accident was a factor in his decision not to run [for president in 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-announcement91-69) Gore stated: "I would like to be President.... But I am also a father, and I feel deeply about my responsibility to my children.... I didn't feel right about tearing myself away from my family to the extent that is necessary in a Presidential campaign."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-announcement91-69) During this time, Gore wrote _[Earth in the Balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth\_in\_the\_Balance "Earth in the Balance")_, a text that became the first book written by a sitting U.S. Senator to make [_The New York Times_ Best Seller list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list") since [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy")'s _[Profiles in Courage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profiles\_in\_Courage "Profiles in Courage")_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)

## First presidential run (1988)

Main article: [Al Gore 1988 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore_1988_presidential_campaign "Al Gore 1988 presidential campaign")

In 1988, Gore sought the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")'s nomination for President of the United States. Gore carried seven states in the primaries, finishing third overall in a field that included Massachusetts Governor [Michael Dukakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Dukakis "Michael Dukakis"), then Senator [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (who would later become Vice President and then President), [Gary Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Hart "Gary Hart"), Congressman [Dick Gephardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Gephardt "Dick Gephardt"), [Paul Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Simon_(politician) "Paul Simon (politician)") and [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson"). Dukakis eventually won the Democratic nomination and went on to lose in a landslide to [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") in the general election.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-70) Although Gore initially denied that he intended to run, his candidacy was the subject of speculation: "National analysts make Sen. Gore a long-shot for the Presidential nomination, but many believe he could provide a natural complement for any of the other candidates: a young, attractive, moderate Vice Presidential nominee from the South. He currently denies any interest, but he carefully does not reject the idea out of hand."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-twoworlds-18) At the time, he was 39 years old, making him the "youngest serious Presidential candidate since John F. Kennedy".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-twoworlds-18)

CNN noted that, "in 1988, for the first time, 12 southern states would hold their primaries on the same day, dubbed 'Super Tuesday'. Gore thought he would be the only serious Southern contender; he had not counted on Jesse Jackson."[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-firstrun-71) Jackson defeated Gore in the [South Carolina primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_Primary "South Carolina Primary"), winning, "more than half the total vote, three times that of his closest rival here, Senator Albert Gore Jr. of Tennessee".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-jacksontriumph-72) Gore next placed great hope on [Super Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Tuesday "Super Tuesday") where they split the Southern vote: Jackson winning Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi and Virginia; Gore winning Arkansas, North Carolina, Kentucky, Nevada, Tennessee, and Oklahoma.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-firstrun-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-pbssuper-73) Gore was later endorsed by New York City Mayor [Ed Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Koch "Ed Koch") who made statements in favor of Israel and against Jackson. These statements cast Gore in a negative light,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-firstrun-71) leading voters away from Gore who received only 10% of the vote in the New York primary. Gore then dropped out of the race.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ said that Gore also lost support due to his attacks against Jackson, Dukakis, and others.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-next-74) Gore was eventually able to mend fences with Jackson, who supported the Clinton-Gore ticket in 1992 and 1996, and campaigned for the Gore-Lieberman ticket during the [2000 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore_2000_presidential_campaign "Al Gore 2000 presidential campaign").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-jacksonendorse-75)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-salonjackson-76) Gore's policies changed substantially in 2000, reflecting his eight years as vice president.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-pbschange-77)

## 1992 vice presidential campaign

See also: [1992 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election") and [Presidential transition of Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_transition_of_Bill_Clinton "Presidential transition of Bill Clinton")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/ElectoralCollege1992.svg/330px-ElectoralCollege1992.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1992.svg)

1992 electoral vote results. The Clinton-Gore ticket won 370–168.

Gore was initially hesitant to be [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")'s running mate for the [1992 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election"); after clashing with the [George H. W. Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_George_H._W._Bush "Presidency of George H. W. Bush") over [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming") issues, he decided to accept the offer.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) Clinton stated that he chose Gore due to his foreign policy experience, work with the environment, and commitment to his family.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-selects-78)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-clintonannounce-79) Clinton's choice was criticized as unconventional because rather than picking a running mate who would [diversify the ticket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticket_balance "Ticket balance"), Clinton chose a fellow Southerner who shared his political ideologies and who was nearly the same age as Clinton.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-selects-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-soil-80) The Washington Bureau Chief for _[The Baltimore Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Baltimore\_Sun "The Baltimore Sun")_, Paul West, later suggested that "Al Gore revolutionized the way Vice Presidents are made. When he joined Bill Clinton's ticket, it violated the old rules. Regional diversity? Not with two Southerners from neighboring states. Ideological balance? A couple of left-of-center moderates. ... And yet, Gore has come to be regarded by strategists in both parties as the best vice presidential pick in at least 20 years."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-wow-81)

Clinton and Gore accepted the nomination at the [Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Convention "Democratic National Convention") on July 17, 1992.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-clintonnom-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-gorenom-83) Known as the _[Baby Boomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby\_Boomer "Baby Boomer") Ticket_ and the _[Fortysomething](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirtysomething\_(TV\_series)#Oxford\_English\_Dictionary "Thirtysomething (TV series)") Team,_ _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ noted that if elected, Clinton and Gore, at ages 46 and 44 respectively, would be the "youngest team to make it to the White House in the country's history".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-selects-78)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-babyboom-84) Gore called the ticket "a new generation of leadership".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-selects-78)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-youth-85) The ticket increased in popularity after the candidates traveled with their wives, Hillary and Tipper, on a "six-day, 1,000-mile bus ride, from New York to St. Louis".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-bustour-86) Al Gore would participate in one vice-presidential debate against Vice President [Dan Quayle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Quayle "Dan Quayle"), and Admiral [James Stockdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stockdale "James Stockdale"). That debate, as of 2023, was the only televised Vice-Presidential debate with more than two participating candidates. The Clinton-Gore ticket beat the Bush-Quayle and Perot-Stockdale tickets with 43% of the popular vote, versus their 38% and 19%, respectively. Clinton and Gore received 370 electoral votes, versus the incumbent ticket's 168, and Perot's 0.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)

## Vice presidency (1993–2001)

Main article: [Vice presidency of Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_presidency_of_Al_Gore "Vice presidency of Al Gore")

See also: [Al Gore and information technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore_and_information_technology "Al Gore and information technology") and [Environmental activism of Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_activism_of_Al_Gore "Environmental activism of Al Gore")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Al_Gore_1993_oath.jpg/250px-Al_Gore_1993_oath.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Al_Gore_1993_oath.jpg)

Gore being sworn in as vice president by Supreme Court Justice [Byron White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_White "Byron White") on January 20, 1993

Al Gore served as vice president during the [Clinton administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton_administration "Clinton administration"). Clinton and Gore were inaugurated on January 20, 1993. At the beginning of the first term, they developed a "two-page agreement outlining their relationship". Clinton committed himself to regular lunch meetings; he recognized Gore as a principal adviser on nominations and appointed some of Gore's chief advisers to key White House staff positions. Clinton involved Gore in decision-making to an unprecedented degree for a vice president. Through their weekly lunches and daily conversations, Gore became the president's "indisputable chief adviser".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/1993_Clinton_Inauguration.jpg/250px-1993_Clinton_Inauguration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1993_Clinton_Inauguration.jpg)

The Clintons and the Gores as [Chelsea Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Clinton "Chelsea Clinton") rings a replica of the [Liberty Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Bell "Liberty Bell"), 1993

Gore had to compete with First Lady Hillary for President Clinton's influence, starting when she was appointed to the health-care task force without Gore's consultation. _Vanity Fair_ wrote that President Clinton's "failure to confide in his vice president was a telling sign of the real pecking order", and reported "it was an open secret that some of Hillary's advisers...nurtured dreams that Hillary, not Gore, would follow Bill in the presidency".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-vanityfair.com-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-politico.com-88)

Gore had a particular interest in reducing "waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government and advocated trimming the size of the bureaucracy and the number of regulations".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) During the Clinton administration, the U.S. economy expanded; according to David Greenberg (professor of history and media studies at [Rutgers University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University")), "by the end of the Clinton presidency, the numbers were uniformly impressive. Besides the record-high surpluses and the record-low poverty rates, the economy could boast the longest economic expansion in history; the lowest unemployment since the early 1970s; and the lowest poverty rates for single mothers, black Americans, and the aged."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-econ-89) According to Leslie Budd, author of _E-economy: Rhetoric or Business Reality_, this economic success was due, in part, to Gore's continued role as an "Atari Democrat", promoting the development of information technology, which led to the [dot-com boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble "Dot-com bubble"). (c.1995–2001).[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-eeconomy-90)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Bill_Clinton_mit_Al_Gore2.jpg/250px-Bill_Clinton_mit_Al_Gore2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Clinton_mit_Al_Gore2.jpg)

Gore and President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") on the [South Lawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Lawn "South Lawn"), August 10, 1993

Clinton and Gore entered office planning to finance research that would "flood the economy with innovative goods and services, lifting the general level of prosperity and strengthening American industry".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-hightech-91) Their overall aim was to fund the development of, "robotics, smart roads, biotechnology, machine tools, magnetic-levitation trains, fiber-optic communications and national computer networks. Also earmarked [were] a raft of basic technologies like digital imaging and data storage."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-hightech-91) Critics claimed that the initiatives would "backfire, bloating Congressional pork and creating whole new categories of Federal waste".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-hightech-91)

During the election and his term as vice president, Gore popularized the term "[Information Superhighway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Superhighway "Information Superhighway")", which became synonymous with the Internet, and he was involved in the creation of the [National Information Infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Information_Infrastructure "National Information Infrastructure").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-hightech-91) Gore first discussed his plans to emphasize information technology at [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA") on January 11, 1994, in a speech at [The Superhighway Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Superhighway_Summit "The Superhighway Summit"). On March 29, 1994, Gore made the inaugural keynote to a [Georgetown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University "Georgetown University") symposium on governmental reform[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-92) with a lecture entitled, "The new job of the federal executive". Gore spoke on how technology was changing the nature of government, public administration, and management in general, noting that while in the past deep hierarchical structures were necessary to manage large organizations, technology was offering more accurate and streamlined access to information, thus facilitating flatter management structures.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-93)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-94) He was involved in a number of projects including [NetDay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NetDay "NetDay") '96 and [24 Hours in Cyberspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_in_Cyberspace "24 Hours in Cyberspace"). The Clinton–Gore administration also launched the first official [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") website in 1994 and subsequent versions through 2000.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-firstweb-95) During 1993 and early 1994, Gore was tapped by the administration to advocate for the adoption of the [Clipper Chip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipper_Chip "Clipper Chip"), a technology developed by the [National Security Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Agency "National Security Agency") designed to provide for law enforcement access to encrypted communications. After political and technical objections, the initiative was essentially dropped.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-96)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-97)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-98)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Phoc96v1.jpg/250px-Phoc96v1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Phoc96v1.jpg)

President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") installing computer cables with Vice President Al Gore on [NetDay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NetDay "NetDay") at [Ygnacio Valley High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ygnacio_Valley_High_School "Ygnacio Valley High School") in Concord, CA. March 9, 1996

Gore was also involved in environmental initiatives. He launched the [GLOBE program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLOBE_program "GLOBE program") on [Earth Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_Day "Earth Day") '94, an education and science activity that, according to _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes\_magazine "Forbes magazine")_, "made extensive use of the Internet to increase student awareness of their environment".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-getsweb-99) In 1998, Gore began promoting a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite") ([Deep Space Climate Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Space_Climate_Observatory "Deep Space Climate Observatory")) that would provide a constant view of the Earth, marking the first time such an image would have been made since _[The Blue Marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blue\_Marble "The Blue Marble")_ photo from the 1972 [Apollo 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_17 "Apollo 17") mission.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-earthviewing-100) During this time, he also became associated with [Digital Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Earth "Digital Earth").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-101)

Gore negotiated and strongly supported the [Kyoto Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Protocol "Kyoto Protocol") to reduce [greenhouse gasses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gasses "Greenhouse gasses"), but said upon his return that the administration would not submit the treaty to the Senate for ratification until it was amended to include "meaningful participation by key developing nations",[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-102)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-kyotospeech-103)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-environinitiative-104) The Senate had previously passed unanimously (95–0) the [Byrd–Hagel Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byrd%E2%80%93Hagel_Resolution "Byrd–Hagel Resolution") (S. Res. 98), which declared opposition to any greenhouse gas treaty which would limit US emissions without similar limits on third-world countries such as China.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-senate.gov-105)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-Text_of_the_Byrd%E2%80%93Hagel_Resolution-106) The Clinton administration left office three years later without having submitted the treaty for ratification.

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Bill_Clinton_%26_Al_Gore_sing_national_anthem_at_1997_inauguration.JPG/250px-Bill_Clinton_%26_Al_Gore_sing_national_anthem_at_1997_inauguration.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Clinton_&_Al_Gore_sing_national_anthem_at_1997_inauguration.JPG)

Vice President Gore and President Clinton during the [second inauguration of Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Bill_Clinton "Second inauguration of Bill Clinton"), January 20, 1997

In 1996, Gore became involved in a ["Chinagate" campaign finance controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_campaign_finance_controversy "1996 United States campaign finance controversy") over his attendance at an event at the [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist "Buddhist")[Hsi Lai Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hsi_Lai_Temple "Hsi Lai Temple") in [Hacienda Heights, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda_Heights,_California "Hacienda Heights, California").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-biosen-32) In an interview on [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC")'s _[Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today\_(NBC\_program) "Today (NBC program)")_ the following year, Gore said, "I did not know that it was a fund-raiser. I knew it was a political event, and I knew there were finance people that were going to be present, and so that alone should have told me, 'This is inappropriate and this is a mistake; don't do this.' And I take responsibility for that. It was a mistake."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-CNNtemple-107) A U.S. Department of Justice investigation into the fund-raising activities had uncovered evidence that [Chinese agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_intelligence_activity_abroad "Chinese intelligence activity abroad") sought to direct contributions from foreign sources to the [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") (DNC) before the [1996 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election"). The [Chinese embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_China_in_Washington,_D.C. "Embassy of China in Washington, D.C.") in Washington, D.C. was used for coordinating contributions to the DNC.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-108)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-109) FBI agents were denied the opportunity to ask President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore questions during Justice Department interviews in 1997 and 1998 and were allowed only to take notes.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-110)

In March 1997, Gore had to explain phone calls which he made to solicit funds for Democratic Party for the 1996 election.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-CNNcalls-111) In a news conference, Gore stated that, "all calls that I made were charged to the Democratic National Committee. I was advised there was nothing wrong with that. My counsel tells me there is no controlling legal authority that says that is any violation of any law."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-PBSmoney-112) The phrase "no controlling legal authority" was criticized by columnist [Charles Krauthammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Krauthammer "Charles Krauthammer"), who stated: "Whatever other legacies Al Gore leaves behind between now and retirement, he forever bequeaths this newest weasel word to the lexicon of American political corruption."[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-charlesk-113)[Robert Conrad Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_J._Conrad "Robert J. Conrad") was the head of a Justice Department task force appointed by [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General")[Janet Reno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Reno "Janet Reno") to investigate Gore's fund-raising controversies. In the spring of 2000, Conrad asked Reno to appoint an [independent counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_counsel "Independent counsel") to continue the investigation. After looking into the matter, Reno judged that the appointment of an independent counsel was unwarranted.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-lehrer1-114)

During the 1990s, Gore spoke out on a number of issues. In a 1992 speech on the [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War"), Gore stated that he twice attempted to get the U.S. government to pull the plug on support to [Saddam Hussein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein "Saddam Hussein"), citing Hussein's use of poison gas, support of terrorism, and his burgeoning nuclear program, but was opposed both times by the Reagan and Bush administrations.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-92speech2-115) In 1998, at a conference of [APEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/APEC "APEC") hosted by [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), Gore objected to the indictment, arrest and jailing of Prime Minister [Mahathir Mohamad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahathir_Mohamad "Mahathir Mohamad")'s longtime second-in-command [Anwar Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anwar_Ibrahim "Anwar Ibrahim"), a move which received a negative response from leaders there.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-APEC-116) Ten years later, Gore again protested when Ibrahim was arrested a second time,[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-summons-117) a decision condemned by Malaysian foreign minister Datuk Seri Dr [Rais Yatim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rais_Yatim "Rais Yatim").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-summons-117)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/ElectoralCollege1996.svg/330px-ElectoralCollege1996.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1996.svg)

1996 electoral vote results. The Clinton-Gore ticket won 379–159.

In the 1996 presidential election, Clinton and Gore both ran for re-election for president and vice-president. They faced Republican Senate Majority Leader [Bob Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dole "Bob Dole"), with his running mate, [Jack Kemp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kemp "Jack Kemp"), a former member of House republican leadership and George H. W. Bush's secretary of Housing and Urban Development. Gore and Kemp debated once, in one of the lowest rated debates in history. Gore held his own against Kemp, and kept President Clinton's large lead against Dole stable. While Bill Clinton's job-approval ratings were around 60%, an April 1999 study by the [Pew Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center "Pew Research Center") for the People found that respondents suffered from "Clinton fatigue" where they were "tired of all the problems associated with the Clinton administration" including the Lewinsky scandal and impeachment. Gore's advisers believed that the "Lewinsky scandal and Bill's past womanizing...alienated independent voters—especially the [soccer moms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer_mom "Soccer mom"), who stood for [traditional values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_conservatism "Social conservatism")". Consequently, Gore's presidential campaign "veered too far in differentiating himself from Bill and his record and had difficulty taking advantage of the Clinton administration's legitimate successes". Gore faced an early challenge by former New Jersey senator [Bill Bradley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bradley "Bill Bradley").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-announce2000-118) Bradley was the only candidate to oppose Gore and was considered a "fresh face" for the White House.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-boyhoodhome-121)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-polls99-122) Gore challenged Bradley to a series of debates which took the form of "town hall" meetings.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-townhall-123) Gore went on the offensive during these debates leading to a drop in the polls for Bradley.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-swing-124)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore#cite_note-clock-125) In the Iowa caucus the unions pledged their support to Gore, despite Bradley spending heavily in that state, and Bradley was much embarrassed by his two to one defeat there. **Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center** (formerly the "Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights" and **Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice and Human Rights**, or **RFK Center**)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-introducing-1) is an American [501(c)(3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501(c)(3)_organization "501(c)(3) organization") nonprofit [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights")[advocacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocacy "Advocacy") organization.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-rfkcen-2)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] It was named after [United States Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate")[Robert F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy "Robert F. Kennedy") in 1968, a few months after [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Robert_F._Kennedy "Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy"). The organization of leading attorneys, advocates, entrepreneurs and writers is dedicated to a more just and peaceful world, working alongside local activists to ensure lasting positive change in governments and corporations. It also promotes human rights advocacy through its RFK Human Rights Award, and supports [investigative journalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_journalism "Investigative journalism") and authors through the RFK Book and Journalism Awards. It is based in New York and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-3) Robert F. Kennedy's daughter, [Kerry Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_Kennedy "Kerry Kennedy"), serves as the organization's President.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Robert F. Kennedy Memorial was originally established as a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization "Non-profit organization") in Washington, D.C., in October, 1968. The [Kennedy family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_family "Kennedy family") and friends looked to memorialize Robert Kennedy's public service following [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Robert_F._Kennedy "Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy") on June 5, 1968, in [Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California"). [Fred Dutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Dutton "Fred Dutton"), a long-time friend and Kennedy ally, was named executive director, and [Peter B. Edelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_B._Edelman "Peter B. Edelman"), a member of Kennedy's senatorial staff, became associate director. The chairman of the executive committee was former U.S. Secretary of Defense [Robert S. McNamara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_S._McNamara "Robert S. McNamara").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Memorial was announced during a press conference at [Hickory Hill in McLean, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickory_Hill_(McLean,_Virginia) "Hickory Hill (McLean, Virginia)"), on Tuesday, October 29, 1968. Kennedy's brother [Ted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy") led the press conference, stating that the organization would be a "living memorial" that would work in areas of poverty, crime, and education in America. He went on to say the Memorial would be "an action-oriented program that we think will carry on his concerns, his actions, his efforts to work on so many of the problems in this country that have no solutions". He was joined at the press conference by his sisters, [Patricia Kennedy Lawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Kennedy_Lawford "Patricia Kennedy Lawford") and [Jean Kennedy Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Kennedy_Smith "Jean Kennedy Smith"), as well as dozens of Kennedy family friends and aides.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-4)

Kennedy's widow [Ethel Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethel_Kennedy "Ethel Kennedy") did not attend the press conference, but was nearby, in a second-floor bedroom of Hickory Hill on doctor's orders, awaiting the birth of her eleventh child. She issued a statement saying it was the hope of her husband's family and friends that the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial would carry forward the ideals he worked for during his lifetime: "He wanted to encourage the young people and to help the disadvantaged and discriminated against both here and abroad, and he wanted to promote peace in the world. These will be the goals of the memorial."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-5)

The memorial and other projects started in Kennedy's memory were later collectively renamed Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-6)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Awards")]

### Human Rights Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Human Rights Award")]

The Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Award was created by [Kathleen Kennedy Townsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathleen_Kennedy_Townsend "Kathleen Kennedy Townsend") in 1984 to honor individuals around the world who show courage and have made a significant contribution to [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") in their country.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In addition to receiving a financial award, laureates can partner with the RFK Center on projects to advance their human rights work, benefiting from the resources and technologies at the foundation's disposal. Some have achieved their goals, some are in exile from their home country. The majority continue to live in their home country and work with the support of the center to establish the human rights they are working for.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Since 1984, awards have been given to 43 individuals and organizations from 25 different countries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The 2009 award was presented by [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-7) In 2009, the RFK Human Rights began a partnership with the [California International Law Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_International_Law_Center "California International Law Center") (CILC) at the [University of California, Davis School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Davis_School_of_Law "University of California, Davis School of Law") focusing on the crisis in [Darfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darfur "Darfur").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-8)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

### Ripple of Hope Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ripple of Hope Award")]

Each year, the Robert F. Kennedy Ripple of Hope Award honors exemplary leaders across [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government "Government"), [business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business "Business"), [advocacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocacy "Advocacy"), and [entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment "Entertainment") who have demonstrated an unwavering commitment to [social change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_change "Social change") and worked to protect and advance [equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_(law) "Equity (law)"), [justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice "Justice"), and [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-14) The name of the award is inspired by Kennedy's [Ripple of Hope speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_speech "Ripple of Hope speech") in 1966.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-ripple2020-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-:0-17)

### Book Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Book Award")]

The Robert F. Kennedy Book Award was founded in 1980, with the proceeds from [Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schlesinger,_Jr. "Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.")'s biography, _Robert Kennedy and His Times_. Each year, the organization presents an award to the book which "most faithfully and forcefully reflects Robert Kennedy's purposes – his concern for the poor and the powerless, his struggle for honest and even-handed justice, his conviction that a decent society must assure all young people a fair chance, and his faith that a free democracy can act to remedy disparities of power and opportunity."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-25)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

### Journalism Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Journalism Award")]

Main article: [Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Journalism_Award "Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award")

The Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award was established in 1968 by a group of reporters covering Kennedy's presidential campaign and "honors those who report on issues that reflect Kennedy's concerns including human rights, social justice and the power of individual action in the United States and around the world."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-27)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] Entries include insights into the causes, conditions and remedies of injustice and critical analysis of relevant public policies, programs, attitudes and private endeavors.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Led by a committee of six independent journalists, the Awards are judged by more than fifty journalists each year. Previous winners include [World News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_World_News "ABC World News") anchor [Diane Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Sawyer "Diane Sawyer").
