**Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center** (formerly the "Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights" and **Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice and Human Rights**, or **RFK Center**)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-introducing-1) is an American [501(c)(3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501(c)(3)_organization "501(c)(3) organization") nonprofit [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights")[advocacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocacy "Advocacy") organization.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-rfkcen-2)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] It was named after [United States Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate")[Robert F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy "Robert F. Kennedy") in 1968, a few months after [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Robert_F._Kennedy "Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy"). The organization of leading attorneys, advocates, entrepreneurs and writers is dedicated to a more just and peaceful world, working alongside local activists to ensure lasting positive change in governments and corporations. It also promotes human rights advocacy through its RFK Human Rights Award, and supports [investigative journalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_journalism "Investigative journalism") and authors through the RFK Book and Journalism Awards. It is based in New York and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-3) Robert F. Kennedy's daughter, [Kerry Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_Kennedy "Kerry Kennedy"), serves as the organization's President.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Robert F. Kennedy Memorial was originally established as a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization "Non-profit organization") in Washington, D.C., in October, 1968. The [Kennedy family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_family "Kennedy family") and friends looked to memorialize Robert Kennedy's public service following [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Robert_F._Kennedy "Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy") on June 5, 1968, in [Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California"). [Fred Dutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Dutton "Fred Dutton"), a long-time friend and Kennedy ally, was named executive director, and [Peter B. Edelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_B._Edelman "Peter B. Edelman"), a member of Kennedy's senatorial staff, became associate director. The chairman of the executive committee was former U.S. Secretary of Defense [Robert S. McNamara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_S._McNamara "Robert S. McNamara").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Memorial was announced during a press conference at [Hickory Hill in McLean, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickory_Hill_(McLean,_Virginia) "Hickory Hill (McLean, Virginia)"), on Tuesday, October 29, 1968. Kennedy's brother [Ted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy") led the press conference, stating that the organization would be a "living memorial" that would work in areas of poverty, crime, and education in America. He went on to say the Memorial would be "an action-oriented program that we think will carry on his concerns, his actions, his efforts to work on so many of the problems in this country that have no solutions". He was joined at the press conference by his sisters, [Patricia Kennedy Lawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Kennedy_Lawford "Patricia Kennedy Lawford") and [Jean Kennedy Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Kennedy_Smith "Jean Kennedy Smith"), as well as dozens of Kennedy family friends and aides.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-4)

Kennedy's widow [Ethel Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethel_Kennedy "Ethel Kennedy") did not attend the press conference, but was nearby, in a second-floor bedroom of Hickory Hill on doctor's orders, awaiting the birth of her eleventh child. She issued a statement saying it was the hope of her husband's family and friends that the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial would carry forward the ideals he worked for during his lifetime: "He wanted to encourage the young people and to help the disadvantaged and discriminated against both here and abroad, and he wanted to promote peace in the world. These will be the goals of the memorial."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-5)

The memorial and other projects started in Kennedy's memory were later collectively renamed Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-6)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Awards")]

### Human Rights Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Human Rights Award")]

The Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Award was created by [Kathleen Kennedy Townsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathleen_Kennedy_Townsend "Kathleen Kennedy Townsend") in 1984 to honor individuals around the world who show courage and have made a significant contribution to [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") in their country.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In addition to receiving a financial award, laureates can partner with the RFK Center on projects to advance their human rights work, benefiting from the resources and technologies at the foundation's disposal. Some have achieved their goals, some are in exile from their home country. The majority continue to live in their home country and work with the support of the center to establish the human rights they are working for.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Since 1984, awards have been given to 43 individuals and organizations from 25 different countries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The 2009 award was presented by [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-7) In 2009, the RFK Human Rights began a partnership with the [California International Law Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_International_Law_Center "California International Law Center") (CILC) at the [University of California, Davis School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Davis_School_of_Law "University of California, Davis School of Law") focusing on the crisis in [Darfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darfur "Darfur").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-8)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

### Ripple of Hope Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ripple of Hope Award")]

Each year, the Robert F. Kennedy Ripple of Hope Award honors exemplary leaders across [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government "Government"), [business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business "Business"), [advocacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocacy "Advocacy"), and [entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment "Entertainment") who have demonstrated an unwavering commitment to [social change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_change "Social change") and worked to protect and advance [equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_(law) "Equity (law)"), [justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice "Justice"), and [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-14) The name of the award is inspired by Kennedy's [Ripple of Hope speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_speech "Ripple of Hope speech") in 1966.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-ripple2020-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-:0-17)

### Book Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Book Award")]

The Robert F. Kennedy Book Award was founded in 1980, with the proceeds from [Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schlesinger,_Jr. "Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.")'s biography, _Robert Kennedy and His Times_. Each year, the organization presents an award to the book which "most faithfully and forcefully reflects Robert Kennedy's purposes – his concern for the poor and the powerless, his struggle for honest and even-handed justice, his conviction that a decent society must assure all young people a fair chance, and his faith that a free democracy can act to remedy disparities of power and opportunity."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-25)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

### Journalism Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Journalism Award")]

Main article: [Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Journalism_Award "Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award")

The Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award was established in 1968 by a group of reporters covering Kennedy's presidential campaign and "honors those who report on issues that reflect Kennedy's concerns including human rights, social justice and the power of individual action in the United States and around the world."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripple_of_Hope_Award#cite_note-27)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] Entries include insights into the causes, conditions and remedies of injustice and critical analysis of relevant public policies, programs, attitudes and private endeavors.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Led by a committee of six independent journalists, the Awards are judged by more than fifty journalists each year. Previous winners include [World News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_World_News "ABC World News") anchor [Diane Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Sawyer "Diane Sawyer").

The [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Nobelpriset_, [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): _Nobelprisen_) are awarded annually by the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences"), the [Swedish Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Academy "Swedish Academy"), the [Karolinska Institutet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karolinska_Institute "Karolinska Institute"), and the [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") to individuals and organizations who make outstanding contributions in the fields of [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry"), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature"), [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), and [physiology or medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-1) They were established by the 1895 will of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel"), which dictates that the awards should be administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation"). An additional prize in memory of Alfred Nobel was established in 1968 by [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank") (Sweden's [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank")) for outstanding contributions to the field of [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences"). Each recipient, a **Nobelist** or _[laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate")_, receives [a gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_medal "Nobel Prize medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma"), and a sum of money which is decided annually by the Nobel Foundation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-2)

## Prize

Different organisations are responsible for awarding the individual prizes; the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awards the Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, and Economics; the Swedish Academy awards the Prize in Literature; the Karolinska Institute awards the Prize in Physiology or Medicine; and the Norwegian Nobel Committee awards the Prize in Peace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-3) Each recipient receives a medal, a diploma and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-2) In 1901, the recipients of the first Nobel Prizes were given 150,782 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), equivalent to 10.8 million SEK in 2023. In 2017, the laureates were awarded a prize amount of 9 million SEK.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-4) The awards are presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") in an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-5)

In years in which the Nobel Prize is not awarded due to external events or a lack of nominations, the prize money is returned to the funds delegated to the relevant prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-Winners1942-6) The Nobel Prize was not awarded between 1940 and 1942 due to the outbreak of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-PeacePrizeArticle-7)

## Laureates

Between 1901 and 2017, the [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prizes "Nobel Prizes") and the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") were awarded 585 times to 923 people and organizations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 892 individuals (including 844 men, 48 women) and 24 organizations.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-8) Six Nobel laureates were not permitted by their governments to accept the Nobel Prize. [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") forbade four Germans, [Richard Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kuhn "Richard Kuhn") (Chemistry, 1938), [Adolf Butenandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Butenandt "Adolf Butenandt") (Chemistry, 1939), [Gerhard Domagk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Domagk "Gerhard Domagk") (Physiology or Medicine, 1939) and [Carl von Ossietzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") (Peace, 1936) from accepting their Nobel Prizes. The [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") forbade [Liu Xiaobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo") from accepting his Nobel Prize (Peace, 2010)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-9) and the government of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") pressured [Boris Pasternak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Pasternak "Boris Pasternak") (Literature, 1958) to decline his award. [Liu Xiaobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo"), [Carl von Ossietzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi") were all awarded their Nobel Prize while in prison or detention.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-10) Two Nobel laureates, [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre "Jean-Paul Sartre") (Literature, 1964) and [Lê Ðức Thọ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Duc_Tho "Le Duc Tho") (Peace, 1973), declined the award; Sartre declined the award as he declined all official honors, and Thọ declined the award due to the situation Vietnam was in at the time.

Seven laureates have received more than one prize; of the seven, the [International Committee of the Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross "International Committee of the Red Cross") has received the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") three times, more than any other.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelFacts-11)[UNHCR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNHCR "UNHCR") (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) has been awarded the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") twice. Also the [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") was awarded to [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") twice, as was the [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") to [Frederick Sanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Sanger "Frederick Sanger") and [Karl Barry Sharpless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Barry_Sharpless "Karl Barry Sharpless"). Two laureates have been awarded twice but not in the same field: [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie") (Physics and Chemistry) and [Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling "Linus Pauling") (Chemistry and Peace). Among the 892 Nobel laureates, 48 have been women; the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize was [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie"), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-WomenLaureates-12) She was also the first person (male or female) to be awarded two Nobel Prizes, the second award being the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, given in 1911.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelFacts-11)

[Nobel laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_laureates "Nobel laureates") receive [a gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_medal "Nobel Prize medal") together with a diploma and (as of 2023) 11 million [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona") (roughly US$1.0 million, €0.95 million).

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Nobel_Prize_winners_2012.jpg/250px-Nobel_Prize_winners_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel_Prize_winners_2012.jpg)

Nobel laureates of 2012 – [Alvin E. Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_E._Roth "Alvin E. Roth"), [Brian Kobilka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Kobilka "Brian Kobilka"), [Robert J. Lefkowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_J._Lefkowitz "Robert J. Lefkowitz"), [David J. Wineland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_J._Wineland "David J. Wineland"), and [Serge Haroche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serge_Haroche "Serge Haroche") – during the ceremony

The [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Nobelpriset_, [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): _Nobelprisen_) are awarded annually by the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences"), the [Swedish Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Academy "Swedish Academy"), the [Karolinska Institutet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karolinska_Institute "Karolinska Institute"), and the [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") to individuals and organizations who make outstanding contributions in the fields of [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry"), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature"), [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), and [physiology or medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-1) They were established by the 1895 will of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel"), which dictates that the awards should be administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation"). An additional prize in memory of Alfred Nobel was established in 1968 by [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank") (Sweden's [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank")) for outstanding contributions to the field of [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences"). Each recipient, a **Nobelist** or _[laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate")_, receives [a gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_medal "Nobel Prize medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma"), and a sum of money which is decided annually by the Nobel Foundation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-2)

## Prize

Different organisations are responsible for awarding the individual prizes; the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awards the Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, and Economics; the Swedish Academy awards the Prize in Literature; the Karolinska Institute awards the Prize in Physiology or Medicine; and the Norwegian Nobel Committee awards the Prize in Peace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-3) Each recipient receives a medal, a diploma and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-2) In 1901, the recipients of the first Nobel Prizes were given 150,782 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), equivalent to 10.8 million SEK in 2023. In 2017, the laureates were awarded a prize amount of 9 million SEK.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-4) The awards are presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") in an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-5)

In years in which the Nobel Prize is not awarded due to external events or a lack of nominations, the prize money is returned to the funds delegated to the relevant prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-Winners1942-6) The Nobel Prize was not awarded between 1940 and 1942 due to the outbreak of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-PeacePrizeArticle-7)

## Laureates

Between 1901 and 2017, the [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prizes "Nobel Prizes") and the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") were awarded 585 times to 923 people and organizations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 892 individuals (including 844 men, 48 women) and 24 organizations.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-8) Six Nobel laureates were not permitted by their governments to accept the Nobel Prize. [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") forbade four Germans, [Richard Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kuhn "Richard Kuhn") (Chemistry, 1938), [Adolf Butenandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Butenandt "Adolf Butenandt") (Chemistry, 1939), [Gerhard Domagk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Domagk "Gerhard Domagk") (Physiology or Medicine, 1939) and [Carl von Ossietzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") (Peace, 1936) from accepting their Nobel Prizes. The [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") forbade [Liu Xiaobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo") from accepting his Nobel Prize (Peace, 2010)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-9) and the government of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") pressured [Boris Pasternak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Pasternak "Boris Pasternak") (Literature, 1958) to decline his award. [Liu Xiaobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo"), [Carl von Ossietzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi") were all awarded their Nobel Prize while in prison or detention.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-10) Two Nobel laureates, [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre "Jean-Paul Sartre") (Literature, 1964) and [Lê Ðức Thọ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Duc_Tho "Le Duc Tho") (Peace, 1973), declined the award; Sartre declined the award as he declined all official honors, and Thọ declined the award due to the situation Vietnam was in at the time.

Seven laureates have received more than one prize; of the seven, the [International Committee of the Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross "International Committee of the Red Cross") has received the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") three times, more than any other.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelFacts-11)[UNHCR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNHCR "UNHCR") (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) has been awarded the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") twice. Also the [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") was awarded to [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") twice, as was the [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") to [Frederick Sanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Sanger "Frederick Sanger") and [Karl Barry Sharpless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Barry_Sharpless "Karl Barry Sharpless"). Two laureates have been awarded twice but not in the same field: [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie") (Physics and Chemistry) and [Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling "Linus Pauling") (Chemistry and Peace). Among the 892 Nobel laureates, 48 have been women; the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize was [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie"), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-WomenLaureates-12) She was also the first person (male or female) to be awarded two Nobel Prizes, the second award being the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, given in 1911.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelFacts-11)

**Desmond Mpilo Tutu** ([/ˈ t uː t uː/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-1) 7 October 1931–26 December 2021) was a South African [Anglican bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_bishop "Anglican bishop") and [theologian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_theology "Christian theology"), known for his work as an [anti-apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_resistance_to_apartheid "Internal resistance to apartheid") and [human rights activist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist"). He was [Bishop of Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Johannesburg "Anglican Diocese of Johannesburg") from 1985 to 1986 and then [Archbishop of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Cape_Town "Anglican Diocese of Cape Town") from 1986 to 1996, in both cases being the first black African to hold the position. Theologically, he sought to fuse ideas from [black theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_theology "Black theology") with [African theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_theology "African theology").

Tutu was born of mixed [Xhosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_people "Xhosa people") and [Motswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tswana_people "Tswana people") heritage to a poor family in [Klerksdorp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klerksdorp "Klerksdorp"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa"). Entering adulthood, he trained as a teacher and married [Nomalizo Leah Shenxane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomalizo_Leah_Tutu "Nomalizo Leah Tutu"), with whom he had several children. In 1960, he was ordained as an Anglican priest and in 1962 moved to the United Kingdom to study theology at [King's College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_London "King's College London"). In 1966 he returned to southern Africa, teaching at the [Federal Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Theological_Seminary_of_Southern_Africa "Federal Theological Seminary of Southern Africa") and then the [University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Botswana,_Lesotho_and_Swaziland "University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland"). In 1972, he became the Theological Education Fund's director for Africa, a position based in London but necessitating regular tours of the African continent. Back in southern Africa in 1975, he served first as [dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_(Christianity) "Dean (Christianity)") of [St Mary's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mary's_Cathedral,_Johannesburg "St Mary's Cathedral, Johannesburg") in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg") and then as [Bishop of Lesotho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Lesotho "Bishop of Lesotho"); from 1978 to 1985 he was general-secretary of the [South African Council of Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Council_of_Churches "South African Council of Churches"). He emerged as one of the most prominent opponents of South Africa's [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") system of [racial segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation "Racial segregation") and [white minority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoritarianism#Dominant_minority "Minoritarianism"). Although warning the [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(South_Africa) "National Party (South Africa)") government that anger at apartheid would lead to racial violence, as an activist he stressed [non-violent protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent_resistance "Nonviolent resistance") and foreign economic pressure to bring about [universal suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_suffrage "Universal suffrage").

In 1985, Tutu became the [Bishop of Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Johannesburg "Anglican Diocese of Johannesburg") and in 1986 the Archbishop of Cape Town, the most senior position in southern Africa's Anglican hierarchy. In this position, he emphasised a consensus-building model of leadership and oversaw the [introduction of female priests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordination_of_women_in_the_Anglican_Communion "Ordination of women in the Anglican Communion"). Also in 1986, he became president of the [All Africa Conference of Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Africa_Conference_of_Churches "All Africa Conference of Churches"), resulting in further tours of the continent. After President [F. W. de Klerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._de_Klerk "F. W. de Klerk") released the anti-apartheid activist [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") from prison in 1990 and the pair led negotiations to end apartheid and introduce multi-racial democracy, Tutu assisted as a mediator between rival black factions. After the [1994 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_South_African_general_election "1994 South African general election") resulted in a [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Nelson_Mandela "Cabinet of Nelson Mandela") headed by Mandela, the latter selected Tutu to chair the [Truth and Reconciliation Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_and_Reconciliation_Commission_(South_Africa) "Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Africa)") to investigate past human rights abuses committed by both pro and anti-apartheid groups. Following apartheid's fall, Tutu campaigned for [gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_by_country_or_territory "LGBT rights by country or territory") and spoke out on a wide range of subjects, among them his criticism of South African presidents [Thabo Mbeki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thabo_Mbeki "Thabo Mbeki") and [Jacob Zuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma "Jacob Zuma"), his [opposition to the Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_the_Iraq_War "Opposition to the Iraq War"), and his view that [Israel's treatment of Palestinians constituted apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_and_apartheid "Israel and apartheid"). In 2010, he retired from public life, but continued to speak out on various issues.

Tutu attracted controversy throughout his career. He was popular among South Africa's black majority and was internationally praised for his anti-apartheid activism, for which he won the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") and other international awards. Conversely, many white South Africans considered him too radical, various anti-apartheid activists deemed him too moderate, and Jewish groups accused him of making [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism") statements.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

### Childhood: 1931–1950

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Childhood: 1931–1950")]

Desmond Mpilo Tutu was born on 7 October 1931 in [Klerksdorp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klerksdorp "Klerksdorp"), [Transvaal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transvaal_(province) "Transvaal (province)"), South Africa.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198822Gish20042Allen20069%E2%80%9310-2) His mother, Aletta Dorothea Mavoertsek Mathlare, was born to a [Motswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tswana_people "Tswana people") family in [Boksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boksburg "Boksburg").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198822Allen200610-3) His father, Zachariah Zelilo Tutu, was from the [amaFengu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fengu_people "Fengu people") branch of [Xhosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_people "Xhosa people") and grew up in [Gcuwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gcuwa "Gcuwa"), Eastern Cape.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198822Allen200610%E2%80%9311-4) At home, the couple spoke the [Xhosa language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_language "Xhosa language").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200611-5) Having married in Boksburg,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200614-6) they moved to Klerksdorp in the late 1950s, living in the city's "native location", or black residential area, since renamed Makoeteng.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200614%E2%80%9315-7) Zachariah worked as the principal of a [Methodist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodism "Methodism") primary school and the family lived in the mud-brick schoolmaster's house in the yard of the Methodist mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish20043Allen200616-8)

[![Image 8: Church of Christ the King](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/ChurchofChristtheKing.jpg/250px-ChurchofChristtheKing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ChurchofChristtheKing.jpg)

The Church of Christ the King in Sophiatown, where Tutu was a server under priest Trevor Huddleston

The Tutus were poor;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198828Gish20043-9) describing his family, Tutu later related that "although we weren't affluent, we were not destitute either".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200621-10) He had an older sister, Sylvia Funeka, who called him "Mpilo" (meaning 'life').[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198822,_29Gish20043Allen200619-11) He was his parents' second son; their firstborn boy, Sipho, had died in infancy.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200619-12) Another daughter, Gloria Lindiwe, was born after him.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198822-13) Tutu was sickly from birth;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish20042Allen200619-14)[polio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio "Polio") atrophied his right hand,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198832Allen200619-15) and on one occasion he was hospitalised with serious burns.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200620-16) Tutu had a close relationship with his father, although angered at the latter's heavy drinking and violence toward his wife.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198822Gish20043Allen200622-17) The family were initially Methodists and Tutu was [baptised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism "Baptism") into the [Methodist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_Church_of_Southern_Africa "Methodist Church of Southern Africa") in June 1932.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198830Gish20044Allen200633-18) They subsequently changed denominations, first to the [African Methodist Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Methodist_Episcopal_Church "African Methodist Episcopal Church") and then to the [Anglican Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church "Anglican Church").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198830%E2%80%9331Gish20044Allen200633-19)

In 1936, the family moved to [Tshing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tshing "Tshing"), where Zachariah became principal of a Methodist school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200620-16) There, Tutu started his primary education,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200621-10) learned [Afrikaans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans"),[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198823Gish20044Allen200621-20) and became the server at St Francis Anglican Church.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200633-21) He developed a love of reading, particularly enjoying comic books and European [fairy tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_tales "Fairy tales").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198830Gish20044Allen200621-22) In Tshing his parents had a third son, Tamsanqa, who also died in infancy.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200621-10) Around 1941, Tutu's mother moved to the [Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witwatersrand "Witwatersrand") to work as a cook at [Ezenzeleni Blind Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezenzeleni_Blind_Institute "Ezenzeleni Blind Institute") in Johannesburg. Tutu joined her in the city, living in [Roodepoort West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roodepoort "Roodepoort").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish20045Allen200624-23) In Johannesburg, he attended a Methodist primary school before transferring to the Swedish Boarding School (SBS) in the [St Agnes Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Martin's_School_(Rosettenville) "St. Martin's School (Rosettenville)").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200624-24) Several months later, he moved with his father to [Ermelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ermelo,_Mpumalanga "Ermelo, Mpumalanga"), [eastern Transvaal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Transvaal "Eastern Transvaal").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200625-25) After six months, the duo returned to Roodepoort West, where Tutu resumed his studies at SBS.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200625-25) Aged 12, he underwent [confirmation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmation "Confirmation") at St Mary's Church, Roodepoort.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200634-26)

Tutu entered the Johannesburg Bantu High School (Madibane High School) in 1945, where he excelled academically.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200625,_34%E2%80%9335-27) Joining a school [rugby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union") team, he developed a lifelong love of the sport.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200636-28) Outside of school, he earned money selling oranges and as a [caddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caddie "Caddie") for white [golfers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golfer "Golfer").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198827Gish20047Allen200637-29) To avoid the expense of a daily train commute to school, he briefly lived with family nearer to Johannesburg, before moving back in with his parents when they relocated to [Munsieville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munsieville "Munsieville").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200636,_37%E2%80%9338-30) He then returned to Johannesburg, moving into an Anglican hostel near the Church of Christ the King in [Sophiatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophiatown "Sophiatown").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198829Gish20048Allen200642-31) He became a server at the church and came under the influence of its priest, [Trevor Huddleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Huddleston "Trevor Huddleston");[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200410Allen200643%E2%80%9345-32) later biographer [Shirley du Boulay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_du_Boulay "Shirley du Boulay") suggested that Huddleston was "the greatest single influence" in Tutu's life.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198831-33) In 1947, Tutu contracted [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") and was hospitalised in [Rietfontein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rietfontein "Rietfontein") for 18 months, during which he was regularly visited by Huddleston.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198829%E2%80%9330Gish20049Allen200645%E2%80%9346-34) In the hospital, he underwent [circumcision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumcision "Circumcision") to mark his transition to manhood.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200647-35) He returned to school in 1949 and took his national exams in late 1950, gaining a second-class pass.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200647%E2%80%9348-36)

### College and teaching career: 1951–1955

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: College and teaching career: 1951–1955")]

Although Tutu secured admission to study medicine at the [University of the Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand "University of the Witwatersrand"), his parents could not afford the tuition fees.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200647%E2%80%9348-36) Instead, he turned toward teaching, gaining a government scholarship for a course at [Pretoria Bantu Normal College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pretoria "University of Pretoria"), a teacher training institution, in 1951.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200412Allen200648-37) There, he served as treasurer of the Student Representative Council, helped to organise the Literacy and Dramatic Society, and chaired the Cultural and Debating Society.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200648-38) During one debating event he met the lawyer—and future president of South Africa—[Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela"); they would not encounter each other again until 1990.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200417Allen200648%E2%80%9349-39) At the college, Tutu attained his Transvaal Bantu Teachers Diploma, having gained advice about taking exams from the activist [Robert Sobukwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sobukwe "Robert Sobukwe").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198837Gish200418Allen200650-40) He had also taken five correspondence courses provided by the [University of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Africa "University of South Africa") (UNISA), graduating in the same class as future Zimbabwean leader [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198837Gish200418Allen200649%E2%80%9350-41)

In 1954, Tutu began teaching English at Madibane High School; the following year, he transferred to the Krugersdorp High School, where he taught English and history.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198837Gish200417,_18Allen200650%E2%80%9351-42) He began courting Nomalizo Leah Shenxane, a friend of his sister Gloria who was studying to become a primary school teacher.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200418Allen200651-43) They were legally married at Krugersdorp Native Commissioner's Court in June 1955, before undergoing a [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholicism "Roman Catholicism") wedding ceremony at the Church of Mary Queen of Apostles; although an Anglican, Tutu agreed to the ceremony due to Leah's Roman Catholic faith.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198838Allen200651%E2%80%9352-44) The newlyweds lived at Tutu's parental home before renting their own six months later.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200652-45) Their first child, Trevor, was born in April 1956;[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200422Allen200653-46) a daughter, Thandeka, appeared 16 months later.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200653-47) The couple worshipped at St Paul's Church, where Tutu volunteered as a Sunday school teacher, assistant choirmaster, church councillor, lay preacher, and sub-deacon;[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200653-47) he also volunteered as a football administrator for a local team.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200652-45)

### Joining the clergy: 1956–1966

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Joining the clergy: 1956–1966")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/St_Albans%2C_Golders_Green-2.jpg/250px-St_Albans%2C_Golders_Green-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Albans,_Golders_Green-2.jpg)

Tutu first ministered to a white congregation at the Church of St Alban the Martyr in Golders Green, living with his family in the curate's flat

In 1953, the white-minority [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(South_Africa) "National Party (South Africa)") government introduced the [Bantu Education Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_Education_Act,_1953 "Bantu Education Act, 1953") to further their [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") system of racial segregation and white domination. Disliking the Act, Tutu and his wife left the teaching profession.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198841%E2%80%9345Gish200420%E2%80%9321Allen200660%E2%80%9361-48) With Huddleston's support, Tutu chose to become an Anglican priest.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200423Allen200661-49) In January 1956, his request to join the Ordinands Guild was turned down due to his debts; these were then paid off by the wealthy industrialist [Harry Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Oppenheimer "Harry Oppenheimer").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200661%E2%80%9362-50) Tutu was admitted to [St Peter's Theological College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Theological_Seminary_of_Southern_Africa "Federal Theological Seminary of Southern Africa") in [Rosettenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosettenville,_Gauteng "Rosettenville, Gauteng"), Johannesburg, which was run by the Anglican [Community of the Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_of_the_Resurrection "Community of the Resurrection").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198846Gish200425Allen200663%E2%80%9364-51) The college was residential, and Tutu lived there while his wife trained as a nurse in [Sekhukhuneland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sekhukhuneland "Sekhukhuneland"); their children lived with Tutu's parents in [Munsieville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munsieville "Munsieville").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200426Allen200664-52) In August 1960, his wife gave birth to another daughter, Naomi.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200668-53)

At the college, Tutu studied the Bible, Anglican doctrine, church history, and Christian ethics,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198847Allen200664%E2%80%9365-54) earning a [Licentiate of Theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licentiate_of_Theology "Licentiate of Theology") degree,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198847-55) and winning the archbishop's annual essay prize.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198862%E2%80%9363Gish200435Allen200672-56) The college's principal, Godfrey Pawson, wrote that Tutu "has exceptional knowledge and intelligence and is very industrious. At the same time, he shows no arrogance, mixes in well, and is popular ... He has obvious gifts of leadership."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200667-57) During his years at the college, there had been an intensification in anti-apartheid activism as well as a crackdown against it, including the [Sharpeville massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharpeville_massacre "Sharpeville massacre") of 1960.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200426Allen200668%E2%80%9369-58) Tutu and the other trainees did not engage in anti-apartheid campaigns;[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198849Allen200670-59) he later noted that they were "in some ways a very apolitical bunch".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200670-60)

In December 1960, [Edward Paget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Paget_(bishop) "Edward Paget (bishop)") ordained Tutu as an Anglican priest at [St Mary's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mary's_Cathedral,_Johannesburg "St Mary's Cathedral, Johannesburg").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198854Gish200428Allen200674-61) Tutu was then appointed assistant curate in St Alban's Parish, [Benoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benoni,_Gauteng "Benoni, Gauteng"), where he was reunited with his wife and children,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198854%E2%80%9355Gish200428Allen200674-62) and earned two-thirds of what his white counterparts were given.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200675-63) In 1962, Tutu was transferred to St Philip's Church in [Thokoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thokoza "Thokoza"), where he was placed in charge of the congregation and developed a passion for pastoral ministry.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198855Gish200428Allen200676-64) Many in South Africa's white-dominated Anglican establishment felt the need for more black Africans in positions of ecclesiastical authority; to assist in this, Aelfred Stubbs proposed that Tutu train as a theology teacher at [King's College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_London "King's College London") (KCL).[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198857Gish200431Allen200677-65) Funding was secured from the [International Missionary Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Missionary_Council "International Missionary Council")'s Theological Education Fund (TEF),[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200681-66) and the government agreed to give the Tutus permission to move to Britain.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200431Allen200679%E2%80%9381-67) They duly did so in September 1962.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198857-68)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Bletchingley_Church_in_September_2010.jpg/250px-Bletchingley_Church_in_September_2010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bletchingley_Church_in_September_2010.jpg)

During his master's degree, Tutu worked as assistant curate at St Mary's Church in Bletchingley, Surrey.

At KCL, Tutu studied under theologians like [Dennis Nineham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Nineham "Dennis Nineham"), [Christopher Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Evans_(theologian) "Christopher Evans (theologian)"), [Sydney Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Evans_(priest) "Sydney Evans (priest)"), [Geoffrey Parrinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Parrinder "Geoffrey Parrinder"), and [Eric Mascall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Mascall "Eric Mascall").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200686-69) In London, the Tutus felt liberated experiencing a life free from South Africa's apartheid and [pass laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pass_laws "Pass laws");[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198858Gish200432Allen200687-70) he later noted that "there is racism in England, but we were not exposed to it".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200687-71) He was also impressed by the [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") in the country, especially at [Speakers' Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speakers'_Corner "Speakers' Corner") in London's [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198859-72) The family moved into the curate's flat behind the Church of St Alban the Martyr in [Golders Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golders_Green "Golders Green"), where Tutu assisted Sunday services, the first time that he had ministered to a white congregation.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198857%E2%80%9358,_63Gish200431,_33Allen200684,_87-73) It was in the flat that a daughter, [Mpho Andrea Tutu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpho_Andrea_Tutu "Mpho Andrea Tutu"), was born in 1963.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200434Allen200688-74) Tutu was academically successful and his tutors suggested that he convert to an [honours degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honours_degree "Honours degree"), which entailed his also studying [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew "Hebrew").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200689%E2%80%9390-75) He received his degree from [Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_The_Queen_Mother "Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother") in a ceremony held at the [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198861-76)

Tutu then secured a TEF grant to study for a master's degree,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198861%E2%80%9362Allen200692-77) doing so from October 1965 until September 1966, completing his dissertation on [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") in West Africa.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200435Allen200692,_95-78) During this period, the family moved to [Bletchingley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bletchingley "Bletchingley") in Surrey, where Tutu worked as the assistant curate of St Mary's Church.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198863Gish200435Allen200693-79) In the village, he encouraged cooperation between his Anglican parishioners and the local Roman Catholic and Methodist communities.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200435-80) Tutu's time in London helped him to jettison any bitterness to whites and feelings of racial inferiority; he overcame his habit of automatically deferring to whites.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200434-81)

## Career during apartheid

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Career during apartheid")]

### Teaching in South Africa and Lesotho: 1966–1972

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Teaching in South Africa and Lesotho: 1966–1972")]

In 1966, Tutu and his family moved to [East Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Jerusalem "East Jerusalem"), where he studied [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") and Greek for two months at [St George's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George's_College,_Jerusalem "St. George's College, Jerusalem").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200439Allen200698%E2%80%9399-82) They then returned to South Africa,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006101-83) settling in [Alice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice,_South_Africa "Alice, South Africa") in 1967. The [Federal Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Theological_Seminary_of_Southern_Africa "Federal Theological Seminary of Southern Africa") (Fedsem) had recently been established there as an amalgamation of training institutions from different Christian denominations.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198869Gish200441Allen2006101,_103-84) At Fedsem, Tutu was employed teaching doctrine, the [Old Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament"), and Greek;[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198873Allen2006104-85) Leah became its library assistant.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006105-86) Tutu was the college's first black staff-member,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006104,_105-87) and the campus allowed a level of racial-mixing which was rare in South Africa.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198871%E2%80%9372Allen2006105-88) The Tutus sent their children to a private boarding school in Swaziland, thereby keeping them from South Africa's Bantu Education syllabus.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200442Allen2006101-89)

Tutu joined a pan-Protestant group, the Church Unity Commission,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006105-86) served as a delegate at Anglican-Catholic conversations,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006116-90) and began publishing in [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006116-90) He also became the Anglican chaplain to the neighbouring [University of Fort Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Fort_Hare "University of Fort Hare");[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200442Allen2006108-91) in an unusual move for the time, Tutu invited female as well as male students to become servers during the [Eucharist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist "Eucharist").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006108-92) He joined student delegations to meetings of the Anglican Students' Federation and the University Christian Movement,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006109-93) and was broadly supportive of the [Black Consciousness Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Consciousness_Movement "Black Consciousness Movement") that emerged from South Africa's 1960s student milieu, although did not share its view on avoiding collaboration with whites.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198875%E2%80%9377Gish200443%E2%80%9344Allen2006109%E2%80%93110-94) In August 1968, he gave a sermon comparing South Africa's situation with that in the [Eastern Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc"), likening anti-apartheid protests to the recent [Prague Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Spring "Prague Spring").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198878Gish200444Allen2006110-95) In September, Fort Hare students held a sit-in protest over the university administration's policies; after they were surrounded by police with [dogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_dogs "Police dogs"), Tutu waded into the crowd to pray with the protesters.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198878%E2%80%9379Gish200444Allen2006111-96) This was the first time that he had witnessed state power used to suppress dissent.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198879Gish200445Allen2006112-97)

In January 1970, Tutu left the seminary for a teaching post at the [University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Botswana,_Lesotho_and_Swaziland "University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland") (UBLS) in [Roma, Lesotho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma,_Lesotho "Roma, Lesotho").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198880Gish200445Allen2006113%E2%80%93115-98) This brought him closer to his children and offered twice the salary he earned at Fedsem.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198881Gish200445Allen2006113-99) He and his wife moved to the UBLS campus; most of his fellow staff members were white expatriates from the US or Britain.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006114%E2%80%93115-100) As well as his teaching position, he also became the college's Anglican chaplain and the warden of two student residences.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006115-101) In Lesotho, he joined the executive board of the Lesotho Ecumenical Association and served as an [external examiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_examiner "External examiner") for both Fedsem and [Rhodes University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_University "Rhodes University").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006116-90) He returned to South Africa on several occasions, including to visit his father shortly before the latter's death in February 1971.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006116-90)

### TEF Africa director: 1972–1975

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: TEF Africa director: 1972–1975")]

> Black theology seeks to make sense of the life experience of the black man, which is largely black suffering at the hands of rampant white racism, and to understand this in the light of what God has said about himself, about man, and about the world in his very definite Word... Black theology has to do with whether it is possible to be black and continue to be Christian; it is to ask on whose side is God; it is to be concerned about the humanisation of man, because those who ravage our humanity dehumanise themselves in the process; [it says] that the liberation of the black man is the other side of the liberation of the white man—so it is concerned with human liberation.

—Desmond Tutu, in a conference paper presented at the Union Theological Seminary, 1973[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006138%E2%80%9339-102)

Tutu accepted TEF's offer of a job as their director for Africa, a position based in England. South Africa's government initially refused permission, regarding him with suspicion since the Fort Hare protests, but relented after Tutu argued that his taking the role would be good publicity for South Africa.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198888Gish200449,_51Allen2006119%E2%80%93120-103) In March 1972, he returned to Britain. The TEF's headquarters were in [Bromley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromley "Bromley"), with the Tutu family settling in nearby [Grove Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grove_Park,_Lewisham "Grove Park, Lewisham"), where Tutu became honorary curate of St Augustine's Church.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198888,_92Gish200451%E2%80%9353Allen2006123,_143%E2%80%93144-104)

Tutu's job entailed assessing grants to theological training institutions and students.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200453Allen2006123-105) This required his touring Africa in the early 1970s, and he wrote accounts of his experiences.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200453Allen2006124-106) In [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire"), he for instance lamented the widespread corruption and poverty and complained that [Mobutu Sese Seko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobutu_Sese_Seko "Mobutu Sese Seko")'s "military regime... is extremely galling to a black from South Africa."[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006125%E2%80%93127-107) In Nigeria, he expressed concern at [Igbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igbo_people "Igbo people") resentment following the crushing of their [Republic of Biafra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biafra "Biafra").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006128-108) In 1972 he travelled around East Africa, where he was impressed by [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta")'s Kenyan government and witnessed [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin")'s [expulsion of Ugandan Asians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_Asians_from_Uganda "Expulsion of Asians from Uganda").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006129%E2%80%93130-109)

During the early 1970s, Tutu's theology changed due to his experiences in Africa and his discovery of [liberation theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_theology "Liberation theology").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006135-110) He was also attracted to [black theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_theology "Black theology"),[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198885Gish200446-111) attending a 1973 conference on the subject at New York City's [Union Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Theological_Seminary_(New_York_City) "Union Theological Seminary (New York City)").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006137-112) There, he presented a paper in which he stated that "black theology is an engaged not an academic, detached theology. It is a gut level theology, relating to the real concerns, the life and death issues of the black man."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006138-113) He stated that his paper was not an attempt to demonstrate the academic respectability of black theology but rather to make "a straightforward, perhaps shrill, statement about an existent. Black theology is. No permission is being requested for it to come into being... Frankly the time has passed when we will wait for the white man to give us permission to do our thing. Whether or not he accepts the intellectual respectability of our activity is largely irrelevant. We will proceed regardless."[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006139-114) Seeking to fuse the African-American derived black theology with [African theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_theology "African theology"), Tutu's approach contrasted with that of those African theologians, like [John Mbiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mbiti "John Mbiti"), who regarded black theology as a foreign import irrelevant to Africa.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006137-112)

### Dean of St Mary's Cathedral, Johannesburg and Bishop of Lesotho: 1975–1978

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Dean of St Mary's Cathedral, Johannesburg and Bishop of Lesotho: 1975–1978")]

In 1975, Tutu was nominated to be the new [Bishop of Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Diocese_of_Johannesburg "Anglican Diocese of Johannesburg"), although he lost out to [Timothy Bavin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Bavin "Timothy Bavin").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198894Gish200454-115) Bavin suggested that Tutu take his newly vacated position, that of the [dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_(religion) "Dean (religion)") of St Mary's Cathedral, Johannesburg. Tutu was elected to this position—the fourth highest in South Africa's Anglican hierarchy—in March 1975, becoming the first black man to do so, an appointment making headline news in South Africa.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198894%E2%80%9396Gish200455,_58Allen2006139,_144%E2%80%93145-116) Tutu was officially installed as dean in August 1975. The cathedral was packed for the event.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006145%E2%80%93146-117) Moving to the city, Tutu lived not in the official dean's residence in the white suburb of [Houghton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houghton_Estate "Houghton Estate") but rather in [a house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutu_House "Tutu House") on a middle-class street in the [Orlando West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_West "Orlando West") township of [Soweto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto "Soweto"), a largely impoverished black area.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198896%E2%80%9397Gish200458Allen2006146-118) Although majority white, the cathedral's congregation was racially mixed, something that gave Tutu hope that a racially equal, de-segregated future was possible for South Africa.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200459%E2%80%9360Allen2006147-119) He encountered some resistance to his attempts to modernise the [liturgies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgies "Liturgies") used by the congregation,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198898Gish200460Allen2006149-120) including his attempts to replace masculine pronouns with gender neutral ones.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198898%E2%80%9399Gish200460-121)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Lesotho_mountain_village_%285285775857%29.jpg/250px-Lesotho_mountain_village_%285285775857%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lesotho_mountain_village_(5285775857).jpg)

As Bishop of Lesotho, Tutu travelled around the country's mountains visiting the people living there.

Tutu used his position to speak out on social issues,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200460-122) publicly endorsing an international [economic boycott of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinvestment_from_South_Africa "Disinvestment from South Africa") over apartheid.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006155-123) He met with Black Consciousness and Soweto leaders,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988102%E2%80%93103Gish200461-124) and shared a platform with anti-apartheid campaigner [Winnie Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnie_Mandela "Winnie Mandela") in opposing the government's [Terrorism Act, 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism_Act,_1967 "Terrorism Act, 1967").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006150-125) He held a 24-hour vigil for racial harmony at the cathedral where he prayed for activists detained under the act.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006150%E2%80%93151-126) In May 1976, he wrote to Prime Minister [B. J. Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._J._Vorster "B. J. Vorster"), warning that if the government maintained apartheid then the country would erupt in racial violence.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988104%E2%80%93106Gish200461%E2%80%9362Allen2006154-127) Six weeks later, the [Soweto uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto_uprising "Soweto uprising") broke out as black youth clashed with police. Over the course of ten months, at least 660 were killed, most under the age of 24.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988106Gish200462%E2%80%9364Allen2006154,_156%E2%80%93158-128) Tutu was upset by what he regarded as the lack of outrage from [white South Africans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_South_Africans "White South Africans"); he raised the issue in his Sunday sermon, stating that the white silence was "deafening" and asking if they would have shown the same nonchalance had white youths been killed.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988107Gish200464Allen2006158-129)
