After seven months as dean, Tutu was nominated to become the [Bishop of Lesotho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Lesotho "Bishop of Lesotho").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200465Allen2006149-130) Although Tutu did not want the position, he was elected to it in March 1976 and reluctantly accepted.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200465Allen2006151-131) This decision upset some of his congregation, who felt that he had used their parish as a stepping stone to advance his career.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200465-132) In July, [Bill Burnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Burnett "Bill Burnett") consecrated Tutu as a bishop at St Mary's Cathedral.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988109Gish200465Allen2006159-133) In August, Tutu was enthroned as the Bishop of Lesotho in a ceremony at [Maseru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maseru "Maseru")'s Cathedral of St Mary and St James; thousands attended, including King [Moshoeshoe II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshoeshoe_II "Moshoeshoe II") and Prime Minister [Leabua Jonathan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leabua_Jonathan "Leabua Jonathan").[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988109Gish200465Allen2006159-133) Travelling through the largely rural diocese,[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988111Allen2006160%E2%80%93161-134) Tutu learned [Sesotho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesotho "Sesotho").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006161-135) He appointed Philip Mokuku as the first dean of the diocese and placed great emphasis on [further education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Further_education "Further education") for the Basotho clergy.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006160-136) He befriended the royal family although his relationship with Jonathan's government was strained.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200466%E2%80%9367Allen2006162-137) In September 1977 he returned to South Africa to speak at the [Eastern Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Cape "Eastern Cape") funeral of Black Consciousness activist [Steve Biko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Biko "Steve Biko"), who had been killed by police.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988117%E2%80%93118Gish200467Allen2006163-138) At the funeral, Tutu stated that Black Consciousness was "a movement by which God, through Steve, sought to awaken in the black person a sense of his intrinsic value and worth as a child of God".[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006164-139)

### General-Secretary of the South African Council of Churches: 1978–1985

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: General-Secretary of the South African Council of Churches: 1978–1985")]

#### SACC leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: SACC leadership")]

> We in the SACC believe in a non-racial South Africa where people count because they are made in the image of God. So the SACC is neither a black nor a white organization. It is a Christian organization with a definite bias in favour of the oppressed and the exploited ones of our society.

—Desmond Tutu, on the SACC[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200475-140)

After John Rees stepped down as general secretary of the [South African Council of Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Council_of_Churches "South African Council of Churches"), Tutu was among the nominees for his successor. John Thorne was ultimately elected to the position, although stepped down after three months, with Tutu's agreeing to take over at the urging of the [synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod") of bishops.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988120Gish200469Allen2006164%E2%80%93165-141) His decision angered many Anglicans in Lesotho, who felt that Tutu was abandoning them.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988121Gish200469-142) Tutu took charge of the SACC in March 1978.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988130Gish200472Allen2006167-143) Back in Johannesburg—where the SACC's headquarters were based at Khotso House[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200474Allen2006170-144)—the Tutus returned to their former Orlando West home, now bought for them by an anonymous foreign donor.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006169%E2%80%93170-145) Leah gained employment as the assistant director of the [Institute of Race Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Institute_of_Race_Relations "South African Institute of Race Relations").[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006170-146)

The SACC was one of the few Christian institutions in South Africa where black people had the majority representation;[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006168-147) Tutu was its first black leader.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200472-148) There, he introduced a schedule of daily staff prayers, regular Bible study, monthly Eucharist, and silent retreats.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006169-149) Hegr also developed a new style of leadership, appointing senior staff who were capable of taking the initiative, delegating much of the SACC's detailed work to them, and keeping in touch with them through meetings and memorandums.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006171-150) Many of his staff referred to him as "Baba" (father).[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200473-151) He was determined that the SACC become one of South Africa's most visible human rights advocacy organisations.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200472-148) His efforts gained him international recognition; the closing years of the 1970s saw him elected a [fellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow#Academia "Fellow") of KCL and receive honorary doctorates from the [University of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kent "University of Kent"), General Theological Seminary, and [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University").[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988169Gish200489%E2%80%9390-152)

As head of the SACC, Tutu's time was dominated by fundraising for the organisation's projects.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988154Gish200473-153) Under Tutu's tenure, it was revealed that one of the SACC's divisional directors had been stealing funds. In 1981 a government commission launched to investigate the issue, headed by the judge [C. F. Eloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frikkie_Eloff "Frikkie Eloff").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988172%E2%80%93177Gish200482Allen2006192%E2%80%93197-154) Tutu gave evidence to the commission, during which he condemned apartheid as "evil" and "unchristian".[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200483%E2%80%9384Allen2006197%E2%80%93199-155) When the Eloff report was published, Tutu criticised it, focusing particularly on the absence of any theologians on its board, likening it to "a group of blind men" judging the [Chelsea Flower Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Flower_Show "Chelsea Flower Show").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988178Allen2006197%E2%80%93199-156) In 1981 Tutu also became the rector of St Augustine's Church in Soweto's [Orlando West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_West "Orlando West").[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988135Gish200475Allen2006215-157) The following year he published a collection of his sermons and speeches, _Crying in the Wilderness: The Struggle for Justice in South Africa_;[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004144-158) another volume, _Hope and Suffering_, appeared in 1984.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004144-158)

#### Activism and the Nobel Peace Prize

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Activism and the Nobel Peace Prize")]

Tutu testified on behalf of a captured [cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_cell_system "Clandestine cell system") of [Umkhonto we Sizwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umkhonto_we_Sizwe "Umkhonto we Sizwe"), an armed anti-apartheid group linked to the banned [African National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_National_Congress "African National Congress") (ANC). He stated that although he was committed to non-violence and censured all who used violence, he could understand why black Africans became violent when their non-violent tactics had failed to overturn apartheid.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006172-159) In an earlier address, he had opined that an armed struggle against South Africa's government had little chance of succeeding but also accused Western nations of hypocrisy for condemning armed liberation groups in southern Africa while they had praised similar organisations in Europe during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War").[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006162%E2%80%93163-160) Tutu also signed a petition calling for the release of ANC activist Nelson Mandela,[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006182-161) leading to a correspondence between the pair.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006183-162)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg/250px-Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg)

US President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") meeting with Desmond Tutu in 1984. Tutu described [Reagan's administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Ronald_Reagan "Presidency of Ronald Reagan") as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks",[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200495-163) and Reagan himself as "a racist pure and simple".[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006255-164)

After Tutu told journalists that he supported an international economic boycott of South Africa, he was reprimanded before government ministers in October 1979.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200477,_90Allen2006178%E2%80%93179-165) In March 1980, the government confiscated his passport; this raised his international profile.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988187Gish200490Allen2006181%E2%80%93182-166) In 1980, the SACC committed itself to supporting [civil disobedience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience "Civil disobedience") against apartheid.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988159%E2%80%93160Allen2006184-167) After Thorne was arrested in May, Tutu and Joe Wing led a protest march during which they were arrested, imprisoned overnight, and fined.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988169Gish200480Allen2006184%E2%80%93186-168) In the aftermath, a meeting was organised between 20 church leaders including Tutu, Prime Minister [P. W. Botha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._W._Botha "P. W. Botha"), and seven government ministers. At this August meeting the clerical leaders unsuccessfully urged the government to end apartheid.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988166%E2%80%93167Gish200481Allen2006186%E2%80%93187-169) Although some clergy saw this dialogue as pointless, Tutu disagreed, commenting: "[Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses "Moses") went to Pharaoh repeatedly to secure the release of the Israelites."[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006188-170)

In January 1981, the government returned Tutu's passport.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200490Allen2006189-171) In March, he embarked on a five-week tour of Europe and North America, meeting politicians including the [UN Secretary-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Secretary-General "UN Secretary-General")[Kurt Waldheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Waldheim "Kurt Waldheim"), and addressing the [UN Special Committee Against Apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_Resolution_1761 "United Nations General Assembly Resolution 1761").[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988189%E2%80%93190Gish200490%E2%80%9391Allen2006189-172) In England, he met [Robert Runcie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Runcie "Robert Runcie") and gave a sermon in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), while in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") he met Pope [John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Paul_II "John Paul II").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988190Gish200491Allen2006190-173) On his return to South Africa, Botha again ordered Tutu's passport confiscated, preventing him from personally collecting several further honorary degrees.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200491Allen2006190%E2%80%93191-174) It was returned 17 months later.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200491-175) In September 1982 Tutu addressed the Triennial Convention of the [Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)") in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") before traveling to Kentucky to see his daughter Naomi, who lived there with her American husband.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988191Gish200491%E2%80%9392-176) Tutu gained a popular following in the US, where he was often compared to civil rights leader [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), although white [conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States") like [Pat Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Buchanan "Pat Buchanan") and [Jerry Falwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Falwell "Jerry Falwell") lambasted him as an alleged communist sympathiser.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988196,_198Gish200493%E2%80%9394-177)

> This award is for mothers, who sit at railway stations to try to eke out an existence, selling potatoes, selling mealies, selling produce. This award is for you, fathers, sitting in a single-sex hostel, separated from your children for 11 months a year... This award is for you, mothers in the KTC squatter camp, whose shelters are destroyed callously every day, and who sit on soaking mattresses in the winter rain, holding whimpering babies... This award is for you, the 3.5 million of our people who have been uprooted and dumped as if you were rubbish. This award is for you.

—Desmond Tutu's speech on receiving the Nobel Peace Prize[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay198817Allen2006213-178)

By the 1980s, Tutu was an icon for many black South Africans, a status rivalled only by Mandela.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200479,_86-179) In August 1983, he became a patron of the new anti-apartheid [United Democratic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Democratic_Front_(South_Africa) "United Democratic Front (South Africa)") (UDF).[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988235Gish200495Allen2006206-180) Tutu angered much of South Africa's press and white minority,[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200478-181) especially apartheid supporters.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200478-181) Pro-government media like _[The Citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Citizen\_(South\_Africa) "The Citizen (South Africa)")_ and the [South African Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Broadcasting_Corporation "South African Broadcasting Corporation") criticised him,[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006202-182) often focusing on how his middle-class lifestyle contrasted with the poverty of the blacks he claimed to represent.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200485-183) He received [hate mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_mail "Hate mail") and death threats from white far-right groups like the [Wit Wolwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barend_Strydom "Barend Strydom").[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200478Allen2006201-184) Although he remained close with prominent white liberals like [Helen Suzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Suzman "Helen Suzman"),[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006203-185) his angry anti-government rhetoric also alienated many white liberals like [Alan Paton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Paton "Alan Paton") and [Bill Burnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Burnett "Bill Burnett"), who believed that apartheid could be gradually reformed away.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006203%E2%80%93205-186)

In 1984, Tutu embarked on a three-month sabbatical at the [General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Theological_Seminary_of_the_Episcopal_Church "General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church") in New York.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988200Gish200495Allen2006211-187) In the city, he was invited to address the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council"),[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200499-188) later meeting the [Congressional Black Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Black_Caucus "Congressional Black Caucus") and the subcommittees on Africa in the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004100-189) He was also invited to the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), where he unsuccessfully urged President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") to change his approach to South Africa.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988207Gish2004100%E2%80%93101Allen2006249%E2%80%93250-190) He was troubled that Reagan had a warmer relationship with South Africa's government than his predecessor [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), describing Reagan's government as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks".[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200492%E2%80%9393,_95-191) Tutu later called Reagan "a racist pure and simple".[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006255-164)

In New York City, Tutu was informed that he had won the 1984 [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"); he had previously been nominated in 1981, 1982, and 1983.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988200Allen2006209%E2%80%93210-192) The Nobel Prize selection committee had wanted to recognise a South African and thought Tutu would be a less controversial choice than Mandela or [Mangosuthu Buthelezi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangosuthu_Buthelezi "Mangosuthu Buthelezi").[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006210%E2%80%93211-193) In December, he attended the award ceremony in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo")—which was hampered by a bomb scare—before returning home via Sweden, Denmark, Canada, Tanzania, and Zambia.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988208Gish2004101%E2%80%93102Allen2006219%E2%80%93220-194) He shared the US$192,000 prize money with his family, SACC staff, and a scholarship fund for South Africans in exile.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006215-195) He was the second South African to receive the award, after [Albert Luthuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Luthuli "Albert Luthuli") in 1960.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200495-163) South Africa's government and mainstream media either downplayed or criticised the award,[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988203Gish200497%E2%80%9398-196) while the [Organisation of African Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity "Organisation of African Unity") hailed it as evidence of apartheid's impending demise.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish200496-197)

### Bishop of Johannesburg: 1985–1986

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Desmond_Tutu&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Bishop of Johannesburg: 1985–1986")]

After Timothy Bavin retired as Bishop of Johannesburg, Tutu was among five replacement candidates. An elective assembly met at [St Barnabas' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Barnabas_College_(Johannesburg) "St Barnabas College (Johannesburg)") in October 1984 and although Tutu was one of the two most popular candidates, the white laity voting bloc consistently voted against his candidature. To break deadlock, a bishops' synod met and decided to appoint Tutu.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988210%E2%80%93211Gish2004105Allen2006217%E2%80%93218-198) Black Anglicans celebrated, although many white Anglicans were angry;[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988212Gish2004105Allen2006218-199) some withdrew their diocesan quota in protest.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988215-200) Tutu was enthroned as the sixth Bishop of Johannesburg in St Mary's Cathedral in February 1985.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004107Allen2006220-201) The first black man to hold the role,[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988210Gish2004105-202) he took over the country's largest diocese, comprising 102 parishes and 300,000 parishioners, approximately 80% of whom were black.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004108-203) In his inaugural sermon, Tutu called on the international community to introduce economic sanctions against South Africa unless apartheid was not being dismantled within 18 to 24 months.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988212%E2%80%93213Gish2004107Allen2006221-204) He sought to reassure white South Africans that he was not the "horrid ogre" some feared; as bishop he spent much time wooing the support of white Anglicans in his diocese,[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988212,_214Allen2006221-205) and resigned as patron of the UDF.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006221-206)

> I have no hope of real change from this government unless they are forced. We face a catastrophe in this land and only the action of the international community by applying pressure can save us. Our children are dying. Our land is bleeding and burning and so I call the international community to apply punitive sanctions against this government to help us establish a new South Africa – non-racial, democratic, participatory and just. This is a non-violent strategy to help us do so. There is a great deal of goodwill still in our country between the races. Let us not be so wanton in destroying it. We can live together as one people, one family, black and white together.

—Desmond Tutu, 1985[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006321%E2%80%93232-207)

The mid-1980s saw growing clashes between black youths and the security services; Tutu was invited to speak at many of the funerals of those youths killed.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988221Allen2006228-208) At a [Duduza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duduza "Duduza") funeral, he intervened to stop the crowd from killing a black man accused of being a government informant.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988221%E2%80%93222Gish2004110Allen2006224%E2%80%93225-209) Tutu angered some black South Africans by speaking against the torture and killing of suspected collaborators.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006226-210) For these militants, Tutu's calls for non-violence were perceived as an obstacle to revolution.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004111-211) When Tutu accompanied the US politician [Ted Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy") on the latter's visit to South Africa in January 1985, he was angered that protesters from the [Azanian People's Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azanian_People's_Organisation "Azanian People's Organisation") (AZAPO)—who regarded Kennedy as an agent of capitalism and [American imperialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_imperialism "American imperialism")—disrupted proceedings.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988217%E2%80%93219-212)

Amid the violence, the ANC called on supporters to make South Africa "[ungovernable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ungovernable_(South_Africa) "Ungovernable (South Africa)")";[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006229-213) foreign companies increasingly disinvested in the country and the [South African rand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_rand "South African rand") reached a record low.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006229%E2%80%93230-214) In July 1985, Botha declared a state of emergency in 36 magisterial districts, suspending civil liberties and giving the security services additional powers;[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988223%E2%80%93224Gish2004111Allen2006227-215) he rebuffed Tutu's offer to serve as a go-between for the government and leading black organisations.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006227-216) Tutu continued protesting; in April 1985, he led a small march of clergy through Johannesburg to protest the arrest of Geoff Moselane.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988220%E2%80%93221-217) In October 1985, he backed the National Initiative for Reconciliation's proposal for people to refrain from work for a day of prayer, fasting, and mourning.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988237%E2%80%93238-218) He also proposed a [national strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_strike "General strike") against apartheid, angering trade unions whom he had not consulted beforehand.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988238%E2%80%93239-219)

Tutu continued promoting his cause abroad. In May 1985 he embarked on a speaking tour of the United States,[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004110-220) and in October 1985 addressed the political committee of the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly"), urging the international community to impose sanctions on South Africa if apartheid was not dismantled within six months.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006231-221) Proceeding to the United Kingdom, he met with Prime Minister [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher").[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDu_Boulay1988224Gish2004113-222) He also formed a Bishop Tutu Scholarship Fund to financially assist South African students living in exile.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004113-223) He returned to the US in May 1986,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2006116-90) and in August 1986 visited Japan, China, and Jamaica to promote sanctions.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGish2004118-224) Given that most senior anti-apartheid activists were imprisoned, Mandela referred to Tutu as "public enemy number one for the powers that be".[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen200679-225)
